questions.prompt: `char buf[10];` Which calls can NEVER write past the end of `buf`?
questions.explain: `fgets` takes the buffer size; `%9s` limits scanf to 9 characters plus the terminator. `gets` and an unbounded `%s` read as much as the user types (this is why `gets` was removed from C11).
option_notes: Bounded by the size you pass.

questions.prompt: `scanf` needs the {{0}} of the variable to store the value in, which is why you write `scanf("%d", &n)`.
questions.explain: `&n` is a pointer to `n`; scanf writes the converted value through it.
`fgets` keeps the newline in the buffer and always adds the terminating `'\0'`. That is why programs often strip it with `line[strcspn(line, "\n")] = '\0'`.

questions.prompt: Which call reads an integer from the keyboard into the variable `n`?
questions.explain: `scanf` needs the ADDRESS of the variable (`&n`) so that it can store the value there. Without the `&` it would write to a random address.
option_notes: Missing `&`: `scanf` would treat the value of `n` as an address.
The first argument of scanf is the format string.
`read` is a system call with other arguments.

questions.explain: Check the return value: `scanf("%d", &n) == 1` means a number was read. A different value means the input was not a number (0) or ended (EOF).
options: The number of items it read and stored (or EOF if the input ended first)
option_notes: The value goes into the variable, not into the return value.
It returns a count, so you can test it.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (`sscanf` reads from a string.)
questions.explain: The first conversion reads 12; the second finds `abc`, which is not a number, so reading stops. `sscanf` returns the number of items converted: 1.
`%s` reads one WORD: it stops at the first white space. To read a whole line use `fgets`.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? (The space in the second format matters.)
questions.explain: `%c` reads the very next character, even a space. A space in the format (`" %c"`) first skips any white space, so the second call reads `x`.
`%d` reads an integer: it takes the `3` and stops at the dot. The `.9` is left unread.

questions.prompt: To read a `double` with `scanf` you use...
questions.explain: `scanf` needs `%lf` for a double (and `%f` for a float). This differs from printf, where `%f` prints a double.
option_notes: `%f` would store a float in memory meant for a double: wrong values.

questions.prompt: Why was `gets` removed from the C standard?
questions.explain: `gets(buf)` has no size argument, so any input longer than the buffer overwrites memory (a classic security hole). Use `fgets(buf, size, stdin)`.
options: It cannot limit the number of characters, so a long line overflows the buffer
option_notes: It did read spaces: it read a whole line.

questions.prompt: After `scanf("%d", &n)` reads `42` the user pressed Enter. What does a following `fgets` return?
questions.explain: `scanf("%d")` does not consume the newline after the number, so the next `fgets` finds it immediately and returns the one-character line `\n`. Read one more character, or use `fgets` + `sscanf` for everything.
options: An empty line (just the leftover newline)
The next line the user types
option_notes: It first sees the newline left behind.
NULL only happens at the end of the input.

questions.prompt: Why does `getchar()` return an `int` and not a `char`?
questions.explain: A `char` has only 256 values, all valid characters. `EOF` is a separate negative number, so the result must be wider. Store it in an `int` and compare with `EOF`.
options: So that it can return EOF (-1), which is different from every character
option_notes: chars can be signed or unsigned; that is not the reason.

questions.prompt: Complete the call so that it never reads more than the size of the buffer.
questions.explain: Passing `sizeof(line)` keeps the size correct even if you change the array's length. `fgets` reads at most size - 1 characters and adds the terminator.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `fgets(buf, size, f)` are true?
questions.explain: `fgets` is the safe line reader: bounded, always terminated, NULL at EOF. It KEEPS the newline in the buffer; remove it yourself if you need to.
options: It reads at most size - 1 characters
It always terminates the buffer with '\0'
It removes the newline from the line
It returns NULL at the end of the input
option_notes: False: the newline stays in the buffer.
